idiom_name: GameObject with std::unique_ptr<Component> slots (classic) or EnTT sparse-set ECS
implementation_notes: The classic C++ form (Game Programming Patterns' own rendering) is an interface per domain - class InputComponent { virtual void update(GameObject&) = 0; } - plus std::unique_ptr members owned by the entity, which makes ownership explicit and deletion of a capability an ordinary reset(). Because each slot is a heap allocation and a virtual call, a fixed capability set is often better stored as values or as a std::variant<PlayerInput, AIInput> slot when you want static dispatch and no allocation. The data-oriented alternative, EnTT, keeps components out of the entity entirely: entt::registry owns per-type pools and registry.view<Position, Velocity>() iterates the packed arrays, trading the entity object for queries and cache-efficient storage.
pitfalls: One unique_ptr slot per capability keeps ownership clear but allocates per entity; hoist assembly out of the frame loop or store the fixed set by value / in a std::variant when the entity is created per frame.
Storing components by value in a std::vector slices derived components and invalidates references when the vector reallocates; hold unique_ptr/pointers or indices instead.

In the EnTT style, adding or removing a component may move elements between packed arrays, so a raw component reference held across an insertion is a dangling reference (enable full pointer stability if you need it).

variants.name: EnTT registry with sparse-set component pools and views
variants.implementation_notes: EnTT removes the entity object: components are stored per type in sparse-set pools inside an entt::registry, entities are typed ids, and behaviour iterates registry.view<...>() over tightly packed arrays. Views are non-intrusive (iteration order is not guaranteed); groups rearrange pools to make a repeated query faster at the cost of extra structure - use them on critical paths only.
pitfalls: Adding or removing components may move elements between packed arrays, so raw references into a pool do not survive a structural change.
Views are snapshots of a query, not a container: creating one per frame is cheap but storing one across structural changes is not.
Entity ids are versioned handles; a recycled id compared by value will silently match a different entity unless you use entt::entity as intended.
